Compare models and forecasts

Source: R/compare.R
mt_compare.Rd

Helpers for the comparisons that most analyses make: several models in one backtest, their scores side by side, and one quantity of several forecasts (models, scenarios, jump-off choices) as a table or a figure.

Usage

mt_compare(
  specs,
  data,
  origins = NULL,
  h = 10,
  n_draws = 200,
  quantities = NULL,
  ...
)

mt_score_table(
  backtest,
  metrics = c("crps", "cov95"),
  targets = NULL,
  by = "model",
  digits = 3,
  hierarchy = NULL
)

mt_compare_forecasts(
  forecasts,
  quantity = c("life_expectancy", "asr", "deaths", "rate", "lifespan_variation"),
  periods = NULL,
  at = NULL,
  ages = NULL,
  strata = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  digits = 1,
  wide = TRUE,
  exposure = NULL,
  measure = "edagger"
)

mt_plot_compare(
  forecasts,
  quantity = c("life_expectancy", "rate", "asr", "lifespan_variation"),
  at = NULL,
  ages = NULL,
  strata = NULL,
  periods = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  data = NULL,
  measure = "edagger"
)

Arguments

specs

A named list of model specifications (or of list(spec = , prep = )).

data

Observed data shown as points (mt_plot_compare(); default: the training data of the first forecast).

origins, h, n_draws, quantities

Passed to mt_backtest().

...

Further arguments of mt_backtest().

backtest

An mt_backtest() result.

metrics

Score columns of mt_score(), for example "crps", "rmse", "cov80", "cov95".

targets

Targets to show (default: all in the backtest).

by

Columns that define the rows (default "model").

digits

Significant digits (mt_score_table()) or decimals (mt_compare_forecasts()).

hierarchy

Optional mt_hierarchy(): scores are then given separately for the bottom series, the aggregates and the grand total (column level).

forecasts

A named list of mt_draws objects or mt_data objects (observed values).

quantity

"life_expectancy", "asr" (per 100,000), "deaths" (summed over the ages, with the exposures of the last observed year unless exposure is given; forecasts only), "rate" (death rates of the ages in ages) or "lifespan_variation" (the index measure of lifespan_variation()).

periods

Years shown (for the plot a range c(first, last), or one year: then medians and intervals per stratum side by side).

at

Age for life expectancy and lifespan variation.

ages

Age labels for quantity = "rate".

strata

Stratum labels shown (default all).

level

Level of the central interval.

wide

One column per forecast (TRUE) or a long table.

exposure

Future exposures for quantity = "deaths" (see mt_deaths()).

measure

Index of lifespan variation for quantity = "lifespan_variation" (see lifespan_variation()).

Value

mt_compare(): an mt_backtest table. mt_score_table(), mt_compare_forecasts(): a data.table. mt_plot_compare(): a ggplot object.

Details

  • mt_compare() runs mt_backtest() for each specification in a named list on the same data and origins and returns one backtest whose model column holds the names (in the order given). An element can be a model specification or list(spec = , prep = ) with its own preprocessing. Without origins, the default origins of mt_backtest() are chosen once for all models, with enough training years for the model that needs the most.

  • mt_score_table() gives the mean scores of a backtest for every target it holds side by side: log death rates without suffix, life expectancy with _le (years), the age-standardised rate with _asr, and differences between strata (contrast in mt_backtest()) with _le_gap and _asr_gap. The same model with different preprocessing gets one row per pipeline (column prep, as in mt_score()).

  • mt_compare_forecasts() gives one quantity of several forecasts (mt_draws) or observed data (mt_data, with Poisson intervals) as "median (lower-upper)", one column per forecast (empty where a forecast has no value for the periods shown).

  • mt_plot_compare() draws the same quantity of several forecasts in one figure, one colour per forecast: medians (dashed), intervals, fitted values (solid) and the observed values (points). With periods around the last observed year it shows the jump-off of each forecast.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1990:2012)
models <- list("random walk" = rwd(), "Lee-Carter" = lee_carter())
bt <- mt_compare(models, x, origins = c(2005, 2007), h = 5, n_draws = 50,
                 quantities = "life_expectancy")
mt_score_table(bt)
#>          model   crps cov95 crps_le cov95_le
#>         <fctr>  <num> <num>   <num>    <num>
#> 1: random walk 0.0564 0.948  0.0801        1
#> 2:  Lee-Carter 0.0355 0.907  0.0746        1
fc <- list("random walk" = mt_forecast(mt_fit(rwd(), x), h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1),
           "Lee-Carter" = mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1))
mt_compare_forecasts(fc, periods = 2022)
#> Key: <label, period>
#>     label period      random walk       Lee-Carter
#>    <char>  <num>           <char>           <char>
#> 1: female   2022 56.4 (55.7-56.8) 56.6 (56.1-57.0)
#> 2:   male   2022 52.1 (51.4-52.8) 52.2 (51.4-53.0)
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) mt_plot_compare(fc, data = x)
